Desert hedgehogs maintain a resting metabolic rate of 113.3 milliliters per hour [JOi = 113.3 milliliters per hour] when measured under stable thermal conditions at 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], a value that aligns closely with expectations for an insectivorous mammal of modest body size. This basal oxygen consumption was recorded during respirometry trials on post-absorptive individuals resting within their thermoneutral zone. The species exhibits a relatively low mass-specific metabolic demand compared to many other eutherian insectivores, likely reflecting adaptations to the hot, arid environments it occupies across the Sahara and Arabian Peninsula. The thermal regime at which these measurements were obtained corresponds closely to the species' preferred active body temperature, suggesting that routine metabolic expenditures are calibrated to sustain activity under typical environmental conditions. Such physiological tuning is common among small mammals inhabiting deserts, where energy conservation is paramount and even modest elevations in metabolic rate can impose substantial costs during periods of resource scarcity.

At an ambient temperature of 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], reproductive output in this desert-adapted erinaceid is constrained by the harshness of its environment, with females typically producing a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year] containing between one and four pups per litter [N_R_i = between one and four pups per litter]. This low annual fecundity reflects a slow life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring investment over numerical output, consistent with patterns observed in other small mammals inhabiting unpredictable arid landscapes. The synchronization of breeding with seasonal resource pulses is critical, as lactating females must sustain both themselves and their rapidly growing young during a narrow window of food abundance. The timing of parturition is presumably cued by photoperiod and rainfall patterns, ensuring that weaning coincides with peak invertebrate availability. This reproductive restraint, combined with the modest litter sizes documented in field studies, underscores the species' reliance on high juvenile survival rather than high fecundity to maintain stable population densities across its expansive but often marginal habitat.

Neonatal Desert hedgehogs emerge from the birth canal at a remarkably small mass of just 8.5 grams [Wwb = 8.5 grams], a value extrapolated from measurements on the closely related African pygmy hedgehog Atelerix albiventris after adjusting for the larger ultimate body size of Paraechinus aethiopicus. These altricial newborns are blind, sparsely covered in soft spines, and entirely dependent on maternal care during the critical early weeks of life. The low birth mass is typical of eutherian mammals that produce relatively large litters relative to maternal size, although in this species the neonatal mass is modest even by hedgehog standards. Rapid postnatal growth ensures that the suckling juvenile period, during which milk ingestion provides the sole nutritional input, is relatively brief. The transition to nutritional independence occurs once the young have developed sufficiently to process solid prey, marking a pivotal stage in the life cycle of this insectivorous mammal.

The species attains an ultimate adult body mass of 453 grams [Wwi = 453 grams], although field-captured individuals are known to range between 280 and 510 grams depending on local conditions and seasonal fat deposition. This maximum recorded body mass places the Desert hedgehog among the larger members of its genus, with body size varying clinally across its distribution from the Atlantic coast to the Red Sea. Adult mass fluctuates substantially across the year, with individuals accumulating lipid reserves prior to periods of reduced activity during the hottest summer months or during winter torpor. The somatic investment required to achieve this adult mass is considerable, given the limited and unpredictable food resources characteristic of arid ecosystems. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this ultimate mass reflects both genetic constraints and ecological pressures, with larger body size conferring advantages in thermoregulation and fasting endurance at the cost of higher absolute energetic demands.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of the species' resting physiology at 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], key developmental milestones follow a predictable schedule: gestation lasts approximately 37 days [tg = approximately 37 days], an interval consistent with the typical gestation length of small erinaceids. After parturition, the pups are weaned at 40 days after birth [tx = 40 days after birth], a relatively extended nursing period that reflects the altricial condition of the neonates and the need for substantial growth before the transition to independent foraging at a temperature of 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C]. Sexual maturity, defined by the attainment of full gametogenesis and reproductive competence, is reached at 250 days after birth [tp = 250 days after birth], meaning that most individuals born early in the breeding season are capable of reproducing the following year at a temperature of 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C]. The maximum recorded lifespan under natural conditions is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years], a longevity that is notable for a small-bodied insectivore and that underscores the slow pace of life history in this species, with delayed reproduction, modest fecundity, and extended adult survival at a temperature of 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C].
